title: Sharing Tradition
html:
Frank LaPena was a Native American artist, dancer and teacher, and this essay is his attempt to explain something outsiders almost always get wrong: what a tradition actually is. It is not a set of old objects or a list of customs recorded in a book. It is a living relationship between people, their ancestors and the land, and it survives only for as long as somebody keeps doing it — and passing it on.

What the exam wants from this essay

Be able to state LaPena's thesis in one sentence: tradition is a living practice, and knowledge of it carries the responsibility to share it. Then know his four supports for that claim — the role of elders, the place of ceremony, the traditional artist, and the difference between living tradition and museum display.

13.1 About the author

Frank LaPena (1937–2019) was an American artist, poet, dancer, ceremonial leader and university teacher of Nomtipom Wintu descent — the Wintu are an indigenous people of northern California, in the Sacramento River valley. He was born in San Francisco, was sent as a child to government boarding schools of the kind that were designed to separate Native children from their own languages and customs, and came back to his people's traditions as a young man.

He studied art and anthropology, and for many years taught at California State University, Sacramento, where he directed the Native American Studies programme and became Professor Emeritus of Art. He was a painter whose work was widely exhibited, a published poet, and — just as importantly for this essay — an active participant in the dance and ceremonial life of his community. His books include The World Is a Gift (2004), a collection of his poems, essays and paintings.

LaPena therefore writes from two positions at once: as a scholar who knows how outsiders study Native cultures, and as an insider who has taken part in the ceremonies being studied. "Sharing Tradition" comes out of that double position, and much of its quiet force comes from it.

13.2 Summary

What makes a person "traditional"

LaPena begins with a question rather than a definition. Who counts as a traditional person? Not, he argues, whoever knows the most facts about the old ways, and certainly not whoever owns the most old objects. A traditional person is someone who lives the tradition: who takes part in the ceremonies, keeps the obligations, behaves in the way the community expects, and accepts the discipline that goes with all this. Tradition, in his account, is something you do, not something you have.

How tradition is learnt

It is learnt from the elders, and it is learnt slowly. The old people do not hand over information in lessons; they teach by example, by letting a young person be present, by giving small tasks, and by telling stories whose meaning may not be clear for years. Much of what matters is passed on orally — in songs, names, prayers and accounts of what happened long ago — and much of it is learnt through the body, by dancing and by doing, rather than through the head.

This also means that knowledge is earned. A learner has to show patience, respect and steadiness before more is given. Some knowledge is sacred and is not given to everybody at all; certain songs and names belong to particular families or to particular ceremonial roles. To LaPena, this is not secrecy for its own sake. It is the recognition that some things are powerful and can be damaged by careless handling.

Ceremony, art and the world

Ceremony is the heart of the essay. Dances and songs are not entertainment and not performances put on for an audience; they are work that has to be done, and their purpose is to keep the relationship between the people and the natural world in good order — to renew the world, to give thanks, to mark the seasons and the passages of a life.

This changes what "art" means. The traditional artist does not make objects to be admired in a gallery or sold to collectors. Regalia, baskets, feathers, paint and song are made for use, and they carry obligations: how they are made, who may make them, what may be done with them afterwards. An object taken out of that setting, put behind glass and labelled, is no longer the thing it was. It has become information about a tradition rather than a part of one.

LaPena is direct about what follows. When outsiders — anthropologists, collectors, tourists, businesses — take songs, designs and ceremonies out of their community and use them for study, decoration or profit, they are not preserving a culture. They are removing the living part and keeping the shell.

Tradition is not frozen

A common misunderstanding, he says, is that a tradition must stay exactly as it was or it is not "authentic". Living traditions have always changed: new materials are used, new songs are received, practices are adapted to the circumstances of each generation. What has to stay constant is not the outward detail but the relationship — the respect, the purpose and the connection to the ancestors and to the land. A tradition that cannot change is already a museum piece.

Sharing as responsibility

The essay closes on the idea in its title. Because tradition exists only in its practice, each generation holds it in trust rather than owning it. Receiving knowledge from the elders therefore creates a debt, and the debt is paid forward, not back: the receiver is obliged to live the tradition properly and to give it to those who come after. Sharing, in LaPena's sense, is not the same as making everything public. It means teaching the right things to the right people at the right time, which is the only way a tradition can survive.

13.3 The central argument

The thesis. Tradition is not a body of knowledge or a collection of objects but a living practice; it belongs to a community rather than to an individual; and anyone who receives it takes on the responsibility of living it properly and handing it on.

How the argument is built. LaPena does not argue like a debater. He builds by accumulation, laying one observation beside another until the conclusion is already obvious by the time he states it.

  1. He redefines the key term. By asking what makes a person traditional, he moves "tradition" from the category of things known to the category of things done. Everything else follows from this move.
  2. He shows how the knowledge travels. Because tradition is learnt from elders, orally, slowly and by participation, it cannot be separated from the people who carry it. A song written down is not the same as a song sung.
  3. He redefines art in the same way. Ceremonial objects are made for use, and their meaning lies in that use. This supplies the sharpest evidence for the thesis: take the object out of the practice and you are left holding something that looks the same and is not the same.
  4. He removes the obvious objection. If tradition is alive, must it never change? No — living things change. What must not change is the relationship behind the practice.
  5. He draws the conclusion. If a tradition exists only while it is being practised, then keeping it alive is nobody's private business. It is a duty owed to the ancestors who gave it and to the children who have not yet received it.

The quiet warning. Running under the argument is a criticism of outsiders who collect, record, display and sell what belongs to a living community. LaPena rarely raises his voice about it, but the logic of the essay condemns the practice completely: you cannot preserve a tradition by removing it from the only place it can live.

13.4 Themes

Identity. Who a person is, in this essay, is settled by what they take part in. Identity is communal and practical rather than private and declared.

Continuity between generations. The past is not behind the community; it is present in the songs, the names and the ceremonies. The ancestors are participants, not history.

Responsibility. The essay's key word. Knowledge is a trust, and a trust creates duties.

Respect for elders. Authority rests with those who have lived the tradition longest, and the correct attitude of the young is patience.

Human beings and the natural world. Ceremonies exist to keep the relationship with the land, the water, the animals and the seasons in repair. Nature is family, not scenery or resource.

The sacred and the restricted. Not everything may be told to everybody. The essay asks outsiders to accept limits they would rather not accept.

Appropriation and commercialisation. Taking cultural material for study, fashion or profit is treated as a kind of quiet destruction.

Change within continuity. A tradition survives by adapting. Rigid imitation of the past is the opposite of tradition, not its purest form.

13.5 Style and technique

A reflective personal essay. LaPena writes in the first person and from inside. He does not pretend to the neutral voice of an anthropologist; his authority comes from having danced, not from having researched.

Tone. Calm, patient, unhurried, occasionally firm. He is explaining rather than attacking, and the restraint is a strategy: a reader who would resist a protest may accept an explanation.

Definition as a weapon. His central technique is to take a familiar word — tradition, art, sharing, authentic — and quietly replace the reader's definition with his own. The argument is won at the level of vocabulary.

Concrete example instead of abstraction. Dances, songs, regalia, feathers, baskets, the behaviour of elders: the ideas arrive attached to things that can be seen and handled, which keeps a philosophical essay readable.

Inclusive pronouns. "We" and "our" appear throughout, marking him as a member of the community he describes and reminding the reader that this is testimony as much as analysis.

Repetition of key words. Tradition, share, respect, responsibility recur until they carry the weight of the whole argument, in the way that repeated words in a ceremony gather force.

Understatement. The criticism of collectors and researchers is made by implication rather than accusation. He states what a tradition is, and leaves the reader to see what taking it away must therefore do.

Circular structure. The essay ends where its title began — on sharing — so the form of the essay repeats the shape of the thing it describes: a circle in which what is received must be given again.

13.6 Glossary

Word Meaning
tradition a way of doing things handed down within a community from one generation to the next
indigenous belonging naturally to a place; the original inhabitants of a region
Wintu an indigenous people of northern California; LaPena was of Nomtipom Wintu descent
elder an older member of a community, respected for experience and knowledge
ceremony a formal act or series of acts performed on a sacred or important occasion
ritual the fixed order of actions followed in a ceremony
oral tradition knowledge passed on by speech and song rather than in writing
ancestors the people of one's family or community who lived in the past
regalia the special clothing and ornaments worn in a ceremony
sacred set apart as holy; to be treated with reverence
secular not religious; belonging to ordinary daily life
heritage what is inherited from earlier generations
continuity unbroken connection over time
custodian a person responsible for looking after something belonging to others
in trust held on behalf of someone else, to be handed on rather than owned
appropriation taking something that belongs to another culture and using it as one's own
commercialisation turning something into a product to be bought and sold
anthropologist a scholar who studies human societies and cultures
authentic genuine; truly what it claims to be
renewal the act of making something new or whole again
reciprocity the practice of giving in return for what one has received

Chapter summary

  • Frank LaPena (1937–2019), a Nomtipom Wintu artist, dancer and professor, writes from inside the tradition he describes.
  • Thesis: tradition is a living practice, not a collection of facts or objects; it belongs to a community; and receiving it creates the duty to live it and pass it on.
  • A "traditional person" is defined by participation — ceremony, obligation, discipline — not by knowledge or ownership.
  • Tradition is learnt from elders, orally and by doing; knowledge is earned, and some of it is sacred and restricted.
  • Ceremonial art is made for use, not display. An object in a museum has been separated from the only setting that gave it meaning.
  • Living traditions change; what must not change is the relationship behind them. Rigid imitation is not authenticity.
  • Style: reflective first-person essay; calm tone; redefinition of key words; concrete examples; inclusive "we"; understated criticism of collectors and commercial users; circular structure.

Practice questions

Short answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. According to LaPena, who counts as a "traditional" person? [2]
  2. How is traditional knowledge passed from one generation to the next? [2]
  3. Why does LaPena say that knowledge must be earned? [2]
  4. How does the traditional artist differ from the artist who works for a gallery? [2]
  5. Why is a ceremonial object in a museum not the same object? [2]
  6. Does LaPena believe a tradition must never change? Explain. [2]
  7. What does the title "Sharing Tradition" mean in the essay? [2]
Model answers — short questions

1. A traditional person is one who lives the tradition: who takes part in the ceremonies, keeps the obligations that go with them, accepts the discipline of the community and behaves accordingly. Knowing many facts about the old ways, or owning old objects, does not make anyone traditional.

2. It is passed on by the elders, orally and by example — through songs, names, prayers, stories and, above all, through taking part in ceremonies and dances. The learner is present, watches, is given small tasks, and slowly grows into the knowledge instead of being taught it in lessons.

3. Because some knowledge is sacred and powerful, and careless handling can damage both the knowledge and the person. A learner has to show patience, respect and steadiness before more is given; certain songs, names and roles belong to particular families and are not given out generally. Earning it is part of learning to treat it properly.

4. The traditional artist makes things for use — regalia, baskets, songs, paint for a ceremony — under obligations about how they are made and what may be done with them. A gallery artist makes objects to be looked at, judged and sold. The first kind of art has a job to do in the life of a community; the second is complete when it is admired.

5. Because its meaning lay in its use. Once it is taken out of the ceremony, put behind glass and labelled, it is cut off from the people, the purpose and the relationships that made it what it was. It looks the same, but it has become information about a tradition rather than a living part of one.

6. No. He says that living traditions have always changed — new materials, new songs, new circumstances in every generation — and that a tradition which cannot change has already become a museum piece. What must stay constant is not the outward detail but the relationship behind it: the respect, the purpose and the connection to ancestors and land.

7. It means passing the tradition on: teaching the right things to the right people at the right time, so that the practice continues into the next generation. It does not mean making everything public. Because each generation holds the tradition in trust rather than owning it, sharing is a duty owed to the ancestors who gave it and to the children who have not yet received it.

Long answer questions (5 marks each)

  1. State LaPena's central argument in "Sharing Tradition" and show how he builds it. [5]
  2. How does LaPena describe the relationship between art, ceremony and community? Why does he object to ceremonial objects being collected and displayed? [5]
  3. Discuss the style and technique of "Sharing Tradition". How does LaPena persuade a reader who is outside his culture? [5]
Model answers — long questions

1. LaPena's thesis is that tradition is a living practice rather than a body of information or a collection of objects, that it belongs to a community rather than to an individual, and that anyone who receives it takes on the responsibility of living it properly and handing it on. He builds this in five moves. First he redefines the key term: instead of asking what tradition is, he asks who counts as a traditional person, and answers that it is the one who takes part, keeps the obligations and accepts the discipline — so tradition shifts from things known to things done. Second, he shows how the knowledge travels: from elders, orally, slowly, through participation and the body, so that it cannot be detached from the people who carry it. Third, he applies the same test to art: regalia, songs and baskets are made for use in ceremony, which gives him his strongest evidence, because an object removed from its use looks identical and is not the same thing. Fourth, he disposes of the obvious objection — that a real tradition must be unchanging — by pointing out that living things change, and that what must be constant is the relationship, not the detail. Finally he draws the conclusion the reader has already reached: since a tradition exists only while it is practised, keeping it alive is a duty owed backwards to the ancestors and forwards to the children.

2. In LaPena's account the three are not separable. Ceremony is the centre of community life: dances and songs are not entertainment but work that has to be done, to give thanks, to mark the seasons and the stages of a life, and to keep the relationship between the people and the natural world in good repair. Art exists to serve that work. Regalia, feathers, baskets, paint and song are made for use, and they come with obligations — who may make them, how, and what may be done with them afterwards. There is no separate category of "the artist" standing apart from the community and expressing a private vision; the maker is a member with a job. This is exactly why LaPena objects to collection and display. A ceremonial object in a museum has been cut away from the people who used it, the occasion it was used for, and the obligations that surrounded it; what remains behind the glass is the shape of the thing without the thing itself. Worse, the removal is presented as preservation, when in fact it takes the living part away and keeps the shell. The same objection covers songs recorded by researchers, designs borrowed by businesses, and ceremonies watched as tourist spectacle. His position is consistent rather than merely protective: if meaning lies in practice, then anything taken out of practice has lost its meaning, however carefully it is stored.

3. LaPena writes a reflective personal essay in the first person, and his authority is that of a participant rather than a researcher — he has danced, not merely studied. That position governs everything else. The tone is calm, patient and explanatory; he sets out to make an outsider understand rather than to accuse, and the restraint is persuasive, because a reader who would argue with a protest will often accept an explanation. His central technique is redefinition: he takes familiar words — tradition, art, authentic, sharing — and quietly replaces the reader's everyday meaning with his own, so that the argument is largely won at the level of vocabulary before any conclusion is stated. He keeps the essay readable by attaching ideas to concrete things: dances, songs, regalia, baskets, the behaviour of the old people. The pronouns "we" and "our" mark him as a member of the community, turning parts of the essay into testimony. Key words — tradition, respect, responsibility, share — are repeated until they carry the weight of the argument, much as repetition in a ceremony gathers force. Finally, his criticism of collectors, researchers and commercial users is made by understatement: he describes what a tradition is and lets the reader work out what removing it must do. The essay ends on the idea its title began with, closing a circle — which is also the shape of the tradition it describes.

Reference to the context

  1. LaPena argues that a person is not traditional because of what he knows or owns, but because of what he takes part in.(a) What definition of tradition does this imply?(b) Why does the definition matter for the rest of the essay?(c) What responsibility does it place on the individual? [5]
  2. LaPena points out that a ceremonial object placed in a museum case is no longer the object it was.(a) Why does he say this?(b) What criticism of outsiders is implied?(c) What, according to him, is the right way to keep a tradition alive? [5]
Model answers — reference to the context

1. (a) It implies that tradition is a living practice — something done rather than something known or possessed. A tradition exists in ceremonies performed, songs sung, obligations kept and discipline accepted, not in facts stored or objects owned. (b) It matters because every later claim in the essay rests on it. If tradition lives only in practice, then knowledge cannot be separated from the people who carry it, ceremonial art cannot be separated from its use, and a recorded or collected version of a tradition is necessarily a dead one. The definition is the foundation of the whole argument. (c) It makes each person a custodian rather than an owner. Because the tradition exists only while it is practised, the individual who has received it must go on living it properly and must pass it on to those who come after. The responsibility runs in two directions: to the ancestors who handed it down and to the children who have not yet received it.

2. (a) Because the meaning of such an object lay in its use. It was made for a ceremony, under obligations about who could make it and what could be done with it. Behind glass it is separated from the people, the occasion and the relationships that gave it meaning, so what survives is the shape of the thing without the thing itself. (b) The implied criticism is of anthropologists, collectors, tourists and businesses who take songs, designs and objects out of living communities for study, decoration or profit, and then describe what they are doing as preserving a culture. LaPena's logic makes this impossible: they remove the living part and keep the shell. He makes the charge by understatement rather than accusation, which gives it more force. (c) By continuing to practise it. Traditions are kept alive by elders teaching, young people taking part, ceremonies being performed, and knowledge being earned and then passed on at the right time to the right people. Traditions may change their outward details in every generation, and should; what must be preserved is the relationship of respect between the community, its ancestors and the natural world.
